title: State pattern
idea: The State pattern moves each state's behaviour into its own object, so the context changes behaviour by swapping that object, not by switching on a flag.

analogy.text: A phone's side button: when off, it boots; when unlocked, it locks; when locked, it wakes the screen. One button, behaviour set by the mode.
analogy.breaks: A phone has fixed modes; in code each state is a class you add.

points: Each state class implements only the actions legal in that state.
An action returns the next state; the context stores it and delegates again.
Unlike Strategy, states choose their successor; with Strategy, the client chooses.
Use it when many methods switch on one status; skip it for two states.

hero.title: A document moving through its states

steps.caption: `Document` starts in a `Draft` state. `edit` is legal here, so the text changes.
`submit` asks `Draft`, which returns a new `InReview`. The document stores it.
`reject` in review returns a fresh `Draft`, so the document can be edited again.
The author edits and submits again. Same calls, new state objects each time.
`approve` returns `Published`. It overrides nothing, so every action falls to the defaults.
A late `edit` reaches the default method and throws. `Document` needed no `if` for this.

code.title: The problem: status flags
code.caption: An enum status with checks spread across methods. One check is out of date.

walk.text: A bare enum. The behaviour for each status is spread across every method.
`edit` checks one bad status. It predates `PUBLISHED`, so published text stays editable.
Each method repeats a `switch` on status. A new status means revisiting all of them.
The output shows a published document silently changed: no exception, no log.

code.title: The fix: state objects
code.caption: Each state is a class; the document delegates and stores whatever state comes back.

walk.text: Default methods refuse every action. A state overrides only what it allows.
`Draft` allows `edit` and `submit`; `submit` also refuses an empty document.
`InReview` returns the next state from both actions, including the way back.
`Published` overrides nothing, so every action throws with a clear message.
`Document` holds no `switch`. Each method delegates and stores the returned state.
Every transition passes through `move`: the one place for logging or auditing.
The late edit now fails loudly, and the approved text stays unchanged.

pitfalls: Letting outside code set the state field skips every transition rule; keep it private.
Storing per-document data in shared state objects leaks it between documents; keep data in the context.
A missed override in a new state throws on a legal action; test every transition.

quiz.q: Same classes as the demo. What does the last line print?
quiz.why: `reject` is legal in `InReview` and returns a new `Draft`. `name()` uses the simple class name of the current state.

takeaway: Each state object knows its legal actions and the state that follows.
